unmatched_authoritative_jurisdiction_dis: CLEAR only after authoritative, unique worksite-jurisdiction resolution and a current release evaluation
evidence_summary: Current Colorado Constitution article X, section 20(8)(a) expressly prohibits local district income taxes, with district defined in section 20(2)(b) to include local government. City & County of Denver v. Sweet held that article X, section 17 gives the General Assembly exclusive, nondelegable income-tax power and leaves even home-rule cities without authority to impose an income tax; Duffy reaffirmed Sweet and invalidated Denver's percentage earnings tax. Johnson distinguishes permissible flat occupational fees because they are not measured by income, and Rountree preserved that state-law distinction. A percentage or graduated municipal tax calculated from employee wages therefore falls within the prohibited class, while current fixed-dollar employee occupational taxes remain excluded.
limitations: Refresh after a constitutional amendment, a controlling Colorado Supreme Court decision changing the state-law income-tax classification, or enactment of authority that survives the constitutional limits.
Fixed-dollar occupational or head taxes remain excluded from the percentage-of-compensation registry even when employers withhold them.

unmatched_authoritative_jurisdiction_dis: CLEAR only after authoritative, unique worksite-jurisdiction resolution and a current release evaluation
evidence_summary: Texas Constitution article VIII, section 1(f) caps every municipal occupation tax at one-half of the state tax on the same pursuit. Brown v. City of Galveston and Attorney General Opinion JM-1195 apply that formula as a prohibition when the state levies no occupation tax on the pursuit. Conlen Grain classifies a revenue tax on the privilege of carrying on an occupation by its subject, so a percentage employee tax triggered by working in the city is an occupation tax even when measured by wages. Texas levies no state occupation tax on employment or wage earning; article XI, section 5 and Tax Code chapter 302 do not permit a charter or ordinance to exceed the constitutional zero ceiling.
limitations: Refresh after amendment of Texas Constitution article VIII, section 1(f), article XI, section 5, Tax Code chapter 302, creation of a state occupation tax on employment, or controlling appellate law changing the zero-cap or occupation-tax classification rules.

This conclusion is limited to a revenue tax imposed on the employee because the employee works in the municipality; regulatory fees, flat charges, employer-side taxes, and materially different legal incidence require separate classification.

Current section 10-1-203 excludes employees rendering services to employers from its municipal business-tax definition and enumerates other revenue taxes, not employee wages. A complete audit of all 96 current Utah Code title PDFs found no qualifying municipal income, wage, earnings, compensation, payroll, or withholding delegation or adopter; every nonzero phrase/proximity hit was unrelated.
limitations: Refresh after amendment of Utah Constitution article XI, section 5; Utah Code section 10-1-203 or Title 59 chapter 10; a new general-law municipal employee-compensation tax grant; or controlling case law that changes the Moss rule.
This is a current-law authority conclusion, not a claim that the Legislature could never authorize such a tax in the future.
